title: The venom and telopodal defence systems of the centipede Lithobius forficatus are functionally convergent serial homologues
projectDescription: We used a combination of morphological, behavioural, proteomic and transcriptomic data to show that venom and telopodal gland systems of Lithobius forficatus are serial homologues that were convergently weaponized to function in predation and defence.
sampleProcessingProtocol: To identify the composition of venom and defensive secretion, we analyzed reduced, alkylated and trypsin digested venom and secretion by liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). To investigate which sequences are present in the front legs (1–5) and posterior legs (12–15) proteomes we analyzed reduced, alkylated and trypsin digested leg samples after TRIZol RNA extraction. For each, 5 µg sample was reduced and alkylated by drying and re-dissolving in 4 M urea 10% ACN 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate, pH 8. Cystines were reduced by incubating with 5 mM dithiothreitol at 70 °C for 5 min and alkylated with 10 mM iodoacetamide at 37 °C for 90 min. The reduced and alkylated samples were digested by incubating with 30 µg/µL trypsin overnight at 37 °C in 2 M urea 10% ACN 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate, pH 8, at a final substrate to enzyme ratio of approximately 100:1. The digested sample was desalted using a C18 ZipTip (ThermoFisher, USA), dried using vacuum centrifugation, dissolved in 0.5% formic acid (FA), and 2 µg of the digest analyzed on an AB Sciex 5600 TripleTOF equipped with a Turbo-V source heated to 550 °C. Tryptic peptides were fractionated on a Shimadzu (Kyoto, Japan) Nexera UHPLC with an Agilent Zorbax stable-bond C18 column (Agilent, USA) (2.1 x 100 mm, 1.8 µm particle size, 300 Å pore size), using a flow rate of 180 µL/min and a gradient of 1–40 % solvent B (90 % ACN, 0.1 % formic acid [FA]) in 0.1% FA over 60 minutes. MS1 spectra were acquired at 300–1800 m/z with an accumulation time of 250 ms, and selecting the 20 most intense ions for MS2 scans acquired at 80–1400 m/z with an accumulation time of 100 ms and optimized for high resolution. Precursor ions with a charge of +2 to +5 and an intensity of at least 120 counts/s were selected, with a unit mass precursor ion inclusion window of ± 0.7 Da, and excluding isotopes within ± 2 Da for MS/MS.
dataProcessingProtocol: To identify proteins and peptides, we used Protein Pilot v4.4 (AB SCIEX, USA) to search the resulting MS/MS spectra against the translated transcriptomes. While biological modifications were allowed, we did not allow for amino acid substitutions in an attempt to reduce the number of false positive identifications of any similar non-toxin or non-defensive homologues. False positives were identified using decoy-based false discovery rates (FDR) as estimated by Protein Pilot, and only protein identifications with a corresponding local FDR of < 0.5 % were considered significant. We then used custom workflows in Galaxy version 18.09 to extract the sequences of identified toxin and non-toxin like components, and used cd-hit v4.6.8-2017-1208 to cluster identical amino acid sequences. Sequences identified proteomically were first searched against a custom database containing all known centipede toxins using blastp v.2.8.0. Sequences showing no similarity to known centipede toxins were then searched against UniProtKB using blastp and searched against InterPro v.69.0. Geneious v11.1.5 was used for sequence alignment with MAFFT (Algorithm: L-INS-I, Scoring matrix: BLOSUM62, Gap open penalty: 1.53, offset value: 0.123), annotation with InterPro, and blastp searches. Maximum likelihood trees were calculated with IQ-Tree v1.6.6, using ModelFinder to find the best model and ultrafast bootstrap with 10000 replicates. Trees were finally visualized using Archaeopteryx 0.9928 beta (180705). Proteomic data from the leg secretion, venom, leg samples after TRIZol RNA extraction, as well as already published data on centipede venoms was used to identify whether toxin-like sequences were present in the venom, front legs (1-5) proteome, posterior legs (12–15) proteome, or ultimate leg telopodal secretion.
